1.title: Network Policies
1.text: Welcome to Module sixteen: Network Policies. It covers the exam area Services and Networking. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. The model in six sentences. Anatomy. The and versus or trap. Common recipes. Reading and debugging. Practice with six hands-on labs worth forty-four points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Services and Networking (twenty percent). Practice in this module: six labs, forty-four points, about forty-eight minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero with kind net.

1.title: The model in six sentences
1.text: The model in six sentences. The figure shows this: What a Network Policy does. Exam tip: A Pod that no policy selects accepts all traffic; the first policy that selects it makes that direction deny by default.

1.title: The model in six sentences, continued
1.text: The model in six sentences. By default all Pods accept all traffic (and may send all traffic). A Network Policy selects Pods with pod Selector and names the directions it governs in policy Types ( Ingress, Egress, or both). Once any policy selects a Pod for a direction, that direction is default deny for the Pod, and only what the policies allow gets through. Policies are additive: the allowed traffic is the union of all policies that select the Pod. There are no deny rules. Policies are namespaced: a policy protects Pods in its own namespace only. Allowed traffic is described by peers ( from for ingress, to for egress) and ports.

1.text: The and versus or trap (the most tested detail). A dash ( - ) starts a new peer. Two selectors under one dash mean and; two dashes mean or. Lab sixteen point five tests both forms.

1.title: Common recipes
1.text: Common recipes. Deny all ingress to every Pod in a namespace. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: When you restrict egress, always allow D N S on port fifty-three, for both U D P and T C P.

1.title: Common recipes, continued
1.text: Common recipes. (no ingress rules at all). The same with Egress denies all outgoing traffic; with both types in the list it denies both. Allow all ingress: ingress (one empty rule) with policy Types Ingress. Allow from a namespace: namespace Selector match Labels team frontend. Label the namespace if needed: kube control label ns fe team frontend. Every namespace also has the automatic label Kubernetes dot io slash metadata dot name name, handy when you have no label to use. Restrict egress but keep D N S working. Once egress is restricted, Pods can no longer ask Core D N S, so name lookups fail. Always allow port fifty-three in both protocols.

1.title: Common recipes, continued
1.text: Common recipes. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Common recipes, continued
1.text: Common recipes. Allow from the outside world: ip Block cidr two hundred three dot zero dot one hundred thirteen dot zero slash twenty-four; in an Ingress rule use it for clients that are not Pods.

1.title: Reading and debugging
1.text: Reading and debugging. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: A blocked connection times out: check the labels first.

1.title: Reading and debugging, continued
1.text: Reading and debugging. A blocked connection times out (it does not say "connection refused"). Typical bugs: a label typo ( role front versus role frontend; Lab sixteen point four), a selector in the wrong namespace, a missing ports entry, forgetting D N S in an egress policy, or a policy whose pod Selector does not match the target Pods. A Service is not affected by policies: policies act on Pods. A client Pod that is allowed to reach the backend Pods can use the Service name; one that is not allowed times out on both.

1.title: Reading and debugging, continued
1.text: Reading and debugging. Exam tip. Read who is protected ( spec dot pod Selector ), who is allowed in or out ( from or to ) and which ports. Then test with kube control exec... W get -T three: the check is the behavior, and you should see both the allowed case working and the blocked case timing out. Exam tip. To allow another namespace you need a namespace label. If it has none, use Kubernetes dot io slash metadata dot name.

1.title: Lab 16.1: default deny
1.text: Lab sixteen point one: default deny. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace np one, the Pod web (engine X) and the Pod client (busy box) can talk to each other. Create a Network Policy named default deny ingress that blocks all incoming traffic to every Pod in the namespace and allows nothing. Outgoing traffic is not restricted. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 16.1: default deny, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n np one apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then sleep five. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.text: Lab sixteen point two: allow from namespace. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace np two, the Pod api (engine X, port eighty) must accept T C P traffic on port eighty only from Pods in namespaces that carry the label team frontend. Everything else must be denied. The namespace fe has the label team frontend and the namespace other does not. Create one Network Policy named api from frontend in np two. 2.title: Lab 16.3: egress policy
2.text: Lab sixteen point three: egress policy. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace np three, the Pod app (busy box) must only be allowed to send traffic to (a) Pods labelled app db on T C P port eighty and (b) the cluster D N S on port fifty-three (U D P and T C P). All other outgoing traffic from app must be blocked. Create one Network Policy named app egress for the Pod app. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 16.4: fix policy labels
2.text: Lab sixteen point four: fix policy labels. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace np four, the Pod backend should be reachable on port eighty from the Pod frontend (label role frontend ), but requests fail since a Network Policy was added. Fix the Network Policy backend in (keep its name; do not delete or relabel the Pods) so that frontend can reach backend while the Pod intruder (label role intruder ) still cannot. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 16.4: fix policy labels, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n np four get netpol backend in dash o yaml then pipe to grep -A three from. Then kube control dash n np four get pods the show labels flag. Then kube control dash n np four patch netpol backend in the type flag set to json dash p op replace, path slash spec slash ingress slash zero slash from slash zero slash pod Selector, and so on. Then sleep five. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.text: Lab sixteen point five: and versus or selectors. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. 2.title: Lab 16.6: deny all allow dns
2.text: Lab sixteen point six: deny all allow dns. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace np six, the Pod client (busy box) must be locked down completely except for name resolution: block all ingress and all egress for every Pod in the namespace, then allow egress on port fifty-three (U D P and T C P) so that D N S still works. Use Network Policies (one named deny all, one named allow dns ). Afterwards the client must still resolve web dot np six dot svc dot cluster dot local but must not be able to fetch the page from web. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What happens to Pods that no Network Policy selects? Answer: They accept and send all traffic. Question two. What does a policy with pod Selector and policy Types Ingress and no rules do? Answer: It denies all incoming traffic to every Pod in its namespace. Question three. How do two policies that select the same Pod combine? Answer: The allowed traffic is the union of both (policies are additive).

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is the difference between two selectors in one from item and two items? Answer: One item: both must match (and). Two items: either may match (or). Question five. Why must an egress policy usually allow port fifty-three? Answer: Without it Pods cannot resolve names with Core D N S. Question six. How does a blocked connection look to a client? Answer: It times out.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. Which label can you always use to select a namespace? Answer: Kubernetes dot io slash metadata dot name namespace name. Question eight. Does a Network Policy work on every cluster? Answer: No; the C N I (Container Network Interface) plugin must enforce it.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Default: all traffic allowed until a policy selects the Pod. Selected equals deny: for each direction in policy Types; allowed traffic is additive. Peers: pod Selector, namespace Selector, ip Block; same item equals and, new dash equals or. Deny all: pod Selector plus policy Types, no rules. Egress: allow D N S (U D P and T C P fifty-three). Namespace label: Kubernetes dot io slash metadata dot name. Test: kube control exec pod then the command W get -q O- -T three H T T P colon slash slash svc; timeout equals blocked. If this course is helping you, please subscribe to the channel and hit the bell icon, so you get a notification when the next video is out. In the next module, we continue the course.
